summary: Describes how Mobile IPv6 works with the revised IPsec architecture and IKEv2. It updates how the security associations that protect mobility signaling are set up and used. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: When a traveling device talks to its home base, the messages must be locked. This note updates how the locks are made, now that the lock system itself has been improved.

subtitle: How Mobile IPv6 uses the revised IPsec architecture and IKEv2 to protect signaling between a roaming device and its home agent.

tldr.problem: RFC 3776 described how IPsec protects Mobile IPv6 signaling, but the IPsec architecture and IKE were later revised, which changes how policies and security associations should be set up.
tldr.mechanism: This document restates the requirements for mobile nodes and home agents using the revised IPsec architecture, shows example manual and IKEv2-based configurations, and adds EAP authentication and dynamic home address assignment inside IKEv2.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 3776 and is a Proposed Standard. With the Mobility Header message type available as a selector, policies no longer need to be set per interface.

today: RFC 4877 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2007. It updates RFC 3776 and, according to the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why the Update Was Needed
sections.content:
RFC 3776 explains how IPsec protects Mobile IPv6 signaling between a mobile node and its home agent. The IPsec architecture was then revised in RFC 4301, and the Internet Key Exchange protocol was substantially revised and simplified as IKEv2 (RFC 4306).

One change matters a great deal here: the list of IPsec selectors now includes the Mobility Header message type, and also the ICMP message type and code. A policy can therefore tell one Mobility Header message from another by its type, instead of checking whether a message travels on the tunnel between the mobile node and the home agent. It also becomes possible to protect Mobile Prefix Discovery messages without applying the same security associations to all ICMPv6 messages.

This document sets out the new requirements for the home agent and the mobile node, shows the policy and security association entries needed, and explains how IKEv2 sets up the security associations.
sections.eli5: The rules for the locks changed, so the travelers and their home base needed an updated instruction sheet.

sections.title: Packet Formats
sections.content:
The mobile node and the home agent MUST support the packet formats of Section 3 of RFC 3776. This document adds a tunneled form. If the mobile node reverse tunnels all its traffic, including its Mobile IPv6 signaling, the Home Address Option does not have to appear in messages sent to the home agent.

A Binding Update in tunnel mode has an outer IPv6 header (care-of address to home agent), an ESP header in tunnel mode, an inner IPv6 header (home address to home agent), and then the Mobility Header carrying the Binding Update with an Alternate Care-of Address option. The Binding Acknowledgement mirrors this, with the home agent as source and the care-of address as outer destination. Tunneled mobile prefix discovery messages look much the same.

Support for these tunneled formats is optional on both the mobile node and the home agent.
sections.eli5: The secret note can be put in a second envelope addressed from the traveler's permanent address. Using the second envelope is optional.

sections.title: Requirements for Mobile Nodes and Home Agents
sections.content:
The requirements are repeated from RFC 3776 so this document stands on its own. For protection levels, ESP for Binding Updates and Binding Acknowledgements MUST be supported and used. ESP in tunnel mode for the Home Test Init (HoTi) and Home Test (HoT) messages MUST be supported and SHOULD be used, and the same holds for ESP on the ICMPv6 messages for mobile prefix discovery. ESP for payload packets tunneled between the two MAY be supported and used.

Several rules concern policy. Because the Mobility Header message type is now a selector, per-interface security policies are no longer required to protect Mobility Header messages. The home agent MUST be able to stop a mobile node from using its security association to send a Binding Update on behalf of another node, and it uses the Peer Authorization Database (PAD) to tie each node's identity to its home address.

Transport mode protection uses ESP with a non-null authentication algorithm. Anti-replay through the ESP sequence number is optional because Binding Update sequence numbers already give anti-replay protection, though that fails if the home agent loses its binding cache state. Only dynamic keying such as IKEv2 gives complete anti-replay protection. Because the care-of address in the outer header is not covered by ESP, Binding Updates sent away from home MUST carry the Alternate Care-of Address option.

When the care-of address changes after an accepted Binding Update, the home agent MUST send to the new address. Such address changes MUST only be made based on Binding Updates protected by IPsec, or an attacker could redirect traffic.
sections.eli5: Important messages must be sealed and signed. The home base must also check that each traveler only claims its own address, and must only change where it sends mail when a properly sealed letter says so.

sections.title: Selector Granularity and Manual Configuration
sections.content:
Not every IPsec implementation supports fine-grain selectors. The document says implementations are still compatible with it without them, but such implementations are not compliant with RFC 4301. It describes three ways to set up policies:

  • Fine-grain selectors, including the Mobility Header message type. The examples in the document assume this.
  • Protocol-level selectors only. The implementation can spot Mobility Header traffic but not individual messages, so all tunneled Mobility Header messages are protected.
  • No protocol selector. All traffic reverse tunneled through the home agent is protected with ESP in tunnel mode, using a security association with the protocol selector set to any. This also suits a node that tunnels everything for privacy.

Section 6 gives example Security Policy Database (SPD) and Security Association Database (SAD) entries for manual configuration, covering Binding Updates, return routability messages, mobile prefix discovery and payload packets. They are examples only; other entries are fine if they give the required security. The PAD is not used with manual configuration.
sections.eli5: Some locks are fancy and some are simple. The note says how to use each kind, and gives example settings you can copy.

sections.title: Setting Up Security Associations with IKEv2
sections.content:
The mobile node starts an IKEv2 exchange if the security associations it needs are missing. It authenticates to the home agent with a shared secret or, preferably when available, a public-key mechanism. Its identity in the IDi payload can be its home address (ID_IPV6_ADDR), an FQDN (ID_FQDN) or an RFC 822 identifier (ID_RFC822_ADDR); the list is not exhaustive.

In the IKE_AUTH exchange the mobile node puts its home address and suitable selectors in the TSi payload to get security associations for Binding Updates and Acknowledgements. Afterwards it uses CREATE_CHILD_SA exchanges for return routability signaling, mobile prefix discovery and optionally payload traffic. The security associations MUST be based on the home address, so they survive care-of address changes. With certificates, the identity in IDi MUST match the certificate, and a home address there MUST match an iPAddress in the SubjectAltName extension.

When the mobile node moves, the IKE SA may stop being valid. If both sides support the Key Management Capability (K) flag in the Binding Update and Binding Acknowledgement, the IKE endpoints are updated. Otherwise a new IKE SA MUST be negotiated.
sections.eli5: The traveler and home base first agree on a secret handshake. They tie it to the traveler's permanent address, so it still works when the traveler moves to a new place.

sections.title: Using EAP Authentication
sections.content:
Besides signatures and shared secrets, EAP can authenticate the mobile node to the home agent inside IKEv2. The mobile node signals this by sending IDi but leaving out the AUTH payload in its first IKE_AUTH message. The home agent answers with an EAP payload if it is willing. No security associations are created until a later IKE_AUTH exchange after EAP succeeds, and EAP adds at least two round trips.

With EAP the identity in IDi may only be used for AAA routing and picking the EAP method. If the real identity is hidden inside EAP, the home agent MUST get it from the AAA server. A shared key produced by the EAP method, when used to make the AUTH payloads, MUST NOT be used for any other purpose.
sections.eli5: Instead of a fixed secret handshake, the home base can ask a separate gatekeeper to check the traveler. That takes a few extra back-and-forth steps.

sections.title: Dynamic Home Address Configuration
sections.content:
A mobile node can ask for a home address by including a Configuration Payload in IKE_AUTH with a zero-length INTERNAL_IP6_ADDRESS attribute in the CFG_REQUEST. It MAY include several to ask for several addresses. The home agent replies in CFG_REPLY with a 128-bit home address and the prefix length of the home prefix, taken from a local database or a DHCPv6 server on the home link.

The address lasts as long as the IKEv2 security association between the two exists, and rekeying the SA extends it. The mobile node may suggest an address, for example an earlier one. If the home agent replies with a different one, the mobile node MUST stop using the old address.

If the home agent cannot allocate an address it MUST send a Notify Payload with INTERNAL_ADDRESS_FAILURE. The mobile node SHOULD then end the IKE_AUTH exchange, and can retry and auto-configure an address, or switch to another home agent. To get a DNS server from the home link, it can include an INTERNAL_IP6_DNS attribute in the request.
sections.eli5: A traveler can ask the home base to hand out a permanent address. If the home base has none to give, the traveler makes one up or tries a different home base.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document defers to RFC 3775 for the security considerations of using IPsec with Mobile IPv6. It adds one concern: a misbehaving mobile node could create security associations for a home address that belongs to another node. So the home agent should check that the node is authorized for that address before creating the associations.

If the address was assigned dynamically as described in Section 9, the home agent MUST associate it with the identity used in the IKE negotiation, and MAY store it in the SPD entries created for that node. Security considerations for EAP in IKEv2 are in RFC 4306.
sections.eli5: The home base must make sure a traveler cannot pretend to own someone else's address.
